opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where people overestimate how hard it is. When we talk about control techniques like auditing suspicious actions or replacing them, a lot of people picture some huge organisational overhaul. But for the specific case of agent scaffolds, the people building them are already doing most of the plumbing.

Think about what a scaffold is. It's a loop: the model proposes an action, the scaffold executes it, the result goes back to the model. Every one of those actions already passes through code the lab or company controls. So adding a step where another model, maybe a weaker trusted one, looks at the proposed action and assigns a suspicion score is not a big engineering lift. It's probably a few weeks of work for a competent team to get a basic version running. Then you decide on a policy. If the action is in the top fraction of a percent of suspiciousness, you pause and send it to a human to audit. If it's moderately suspicious, you throw it away and resample, or defer to the trusted model's version of the action.

The engineering is not the hard part. The hard parts are more about incentives and attention.

First, latency and cost. Product teams care a lot about agents feeling snappy, and if you add a monitor call to every step, people notice. So you need someone senior to say this is a requirement, not a nice-to-have, or you need to make it cheap enough that nobody bothers to fight it.

Second, the human auditing pipeline. Replacing actions is basically automatic, but auditing means someone has to actually look at flagged trajectories, understand them, and make a judgement. That needs a team, on-call rotations, tooling to make the context legible, and an escalation path for when someone thinks they've found the model doing something sketchy. That's a real organisational commitment, and it's the kind that quietly decays if leadership stops caring.

Third, there's a cultural issue. If the auditors mostly see false positives, which they will at first, they get bored and start rubber-stamping. So you want to seed the pipeline with known-bad examples so you can measure whether your auditors are catching things.

So overall, I think the effort is modest compared to how much risk reduction you buy. My guess is that a lab that decided it wanted this could have a reasonable version deployed internally within a few months. The main question is whether anyone with authority decides it's a priority, and that's why I spend a lot of time trying to make these techniques seem concrete and cheap rather than exotic. If it looks like a normal security engineering project, it's much easier for an organisation to just do it.

r001.rationale: The response says replacement is basically automatic while auditing requires a staffed human pipeline. It does not tentatively assess persuading teams to adopt replacement as the greater organisational hurdle than forwarding logs for auditing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underrated parts of the whole picture. When people think about AI control, they tend to imagine the hard part is the technical research — figuring out which monitoring protocols actually catch a scheming model, how much safety you buy per unit of usefulness you give up, that kind of thing. And that stuff is hard. But I think the thing that's going to be at least as hard in practice is the organisational problem of getting the teams who actually build and operate these agent scaffolds to do any of it.

So picture the situation inside an AI company in a couple of years. You've got internal teams running agents that are doing huge amounts of the ML engineering and research. Those scaffolds are built by product-minded or infra-minded engineers whose job is to make the agents go faster and do more. And then a safety team comes along and says, "Hey, we'd like you to route all the agent's actions through this auditing pipeline, and in some fraction of cases we want to pause and have a human look at it, and in some cases we want to throw out the action the agent proposed and replace it with one from a weaker, more trusted model." From the scaffold team's perspective, that's all cost. It's latency, it's engineering complexity, it's a dependency on another team's infrastructure, and it degrades the thing they're being evaluated on.

And the frustrating part is that the auditing-and-replacing techniques are, in some sense, the cheap ones. Compared to, like, "solve interpretability," these are things you could implement in a few months with a competent team. The marginal cost in compute is modest — you run a trusted model on some subset of actions, you have some humans review a small fraction. But "cheap in principle" doesn't mean "cheap to actually get adopted," because the cost lands on people who aren't the ones who care about the benefit.

So the way I think about the organisational effort is that it splits into a few pieces. One is just making the thing as frictionless as possible. If the control team shows up with a library that the scaffold team can wrap around their agent in an afternoon, and it degrades performance by a few percent, you have a shot. If it's a six-week integration project with a flaky service in the middle, you don't, regardless of how good the safety argument is. So a lot of the work is boring software engineering and making the default easy.

The second piece is that you need some kind of mandate from above. I don't think this happens purely bottom-up. Someone with authority has to say, "Models above this capability level don't get deployed internally without a control protocol," and then mean it when a team says, "but we have a deadline." That's a governance question as much as a technical one. And honestly, I think the realistic version of this is that it gets tied into whatever the company's safety framework says about dangerous capability thresholds — once you're past the point where the model could plausibly do serious damage with the affordances it has internally, control measures become a requirement rather than a nice-to-have.

The third piece, which I find myself increasingly thinking about, is that you need the scaffold teams to not route around the measures. Because a lot of the leverage of these techniques comes from them being applied uniformly. If the agent can do dangerous things through some side channel that isn't audited — some script that one engineer wrote that calls the model directly without going through the monitored path — then you've lost a lot. And you can't fully enforce that technically; some of it is culture, some of it is making people understand why it matters.

So in terms of effort, I'd guess the technical work of building a decent auditing-and-replacing setup is, I don't know, a modest team for a year or so. The organisational work of getting it actually used everywhere it should be used is probably comparable or larger, and it's much less legible — you can't write a paper about it. Which is part of why I think it's neglected. People in safety research gravitate toward the parts that look like research. But if you're inside a lab and you care about this going well, I'd argue spending your time on the "how do we actually make teams do this" question is one of the highest-value things you could do, even though it mostly looks like meetings and writing internal docs and building unglamorous tooling.

And the thing I want to flag is that I don't think this is hopeless. Companies do manage to get engineering orgs to adopt security practices, code review requirements, that kind of thing, even when individual engineers would rather not. It's not easy, and it's never perfectly applied, but it's a solved-enough problem that there's a playbook. The question is whether AI companies decide to treat control measures the way they treat security — as a baseline requirement — or the way they treat, like, documentation, which everyone agrees is good and nobody actually does.

r001.rationale: The response describes organizational barriers to adopting auditing and replacement together, but it does not compare the difficulty of adopting replacement with the difficulty of forwarding logs for auditing.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the work is organisational rather than technical. It’s one thing to demonstrate an auditing technique; it’s another to get the team building an agent scaffold to make it part of their workflow, pay the costs, and actually act when it flags something.

You want auditing and replacing to be easy for those teams to adopt. Ideally, they have a standard interface and infrastructure that handles most of the work, rather than each team having to invent its own approach. But someone still needs to own the decision about when an audit is required and what happens as a result. If the team is under pressure to make the agent work better, a safety measure that adds friction can easily get postponed.

So I’d want to work closely with a scaffold team, get something working in their actual setup, and learn where the obstacles are. I wouldn’t assume that producing a good technical proposal is enough to get it adopted.

r001.rationale: The response describes organizational obstacles to adopting auditing and replacing, but it does not compare the difficulty of persuading teams to adopt replacement with the difficulty of forwarding logs for auditing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the work is organisational rather than technical. It’s one thing to show that an auditor can catch a suspicious action in a demonstration. It’s another to get the team building the agent scaffold to route the relevant actions through that auditor, maintain the checks as the scaffold changes, and actually stop or replace the agent when something gets flagged.

The scaffold team is mostly trying to make the agent useful. So if adopting your safety measure means a substantial integration project, or makes failures harder to debug, or adds a lot of latency, you should expect friction. You want to make the safe thing easy to adopt, and you want someone to clearly own making sure it stays in place.

And replacement needs to be a real option. If the team has organised everything around one particular agent, then ‘replace it when it behaves suspiciously’ might be quite an expensive instruction to follow. You’d like to build and test that ability in advance. So I wouldn’t think of this as just handing teams an auditing tool. It’s getting the tool, the workflow, and the incentives to line up.

r001.rationale: The response describes organizational friction around auditing and says replacing an agent may be expensive, but it does not compare persuading teams to adopt replacement with persuading them to forward logs for auditing.
